To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prenatal diagnosis of infantile Sandhoff disease was achieved by the detection of N‐Acetylglucosamyl oligosaccharide accumulation in amniotic fluids using high performance liquid chromotography (HPLC).
the presence of N‐acetylgalactosaminyl oligosaccharide in amniotic ﬂuid was detected by HPLC and that the oligosaccha‐ride levels were 1/100 of those in urine.
Prenatal diagnosis is possible for infantile and juvenile forms of Sandhoff disease by detection of N-acetylglucosaminyloigosaccharides using HPLC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a prenatal diagnostic procedure for the infantile and juvenile forms of GM 2 ganglio‐sidosis (Sandhoff disease).
the development of a prenatal diagnosis test for Sandhoff disease.
the development of a new method for the prenatal diagnosis of infantile Sandhoff disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amniotic‐fluid assay is a useful tool for the prenatal detection of Sandhoff disease and that the assay is applicable to other lysosomal storage disorders.
the amniotic fluids of the two pregnancies in question contained oligosaccharide profiles characteristic of the infantile form of Sandhoff disease.
the amniotic fluids from the fetus at risk contained oligosaccharide material which was identical to that obtained from urine of patients with Sandhoff disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oligosacchrides are present at 16 weeks and the levels increase with gestation.
we are able to detect and quantify the oligosaccherides from amniotic fluid.
prenatal diagnosis of infantile Sandhoff disease can be achieved by the detection and analysis of oligosaccharide excretion in amniotic fluids.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the amniotic fluids of patients with Sandhoff disease contain oligosaccharide species that are similar in size and composition to those found in urine from patients with Sandhoff and Tay‐Sachs diseases.
it’s possible to diagnose this disease in a fetus.
it’s important to be able to identify and treat Sandhoff disease early on, so that children can have the best possible quality of life.
